1	# Stage-3 proof: repaired PML candidates and dissipative-energy classification
     2	
     3	Problem id: `2d_maxwell_pml_energy_functional_exploration`
     4	
     5	Task: `task-stage3-repaired-model-energy`
     6	
     7	## Input fact from the matching test
     8	
     9	The v2 covariantly damped Maxwell--Debye model has the verified stage-2 monotone
    10	energy identity, but the stage-3 interface calculation shows that it is not a
    11	perfectly matched layer.  In an \(x\)-layer with \(\rho_x=\rho>0,\rho_y=0\),
    12	\[
    13	Y_{v2}^2-Y_0^2
    14	=-\frac{\rho}{\mu^2}\left[
    15	\frac{\mu\chi\tau}{(1+\tau s)(1+\tau(s+\rho))}
    16	+\frac{k_y^2}{s^2(s+\rho)}
    17	\right],
    18	\]
    19	so the v2 reflection coefficient is not identically zero.
    20	
    21	Therefore a repaired model must keep the physical Debye law as a function of the
    22	Laplace variable \(s\), not \(s+\rho\), and must implement damping through
    23	coordinate stretching or an equivalent split/ADE system.
    24	
    25	## Candidate 1: classical stretched-coordinate Maxwell--Debye PML
    26	
    27	Let
    28	\[
    29	\varepsilon_D(s)=\epsilon_0\epsilon_\infty+\frac{\chi}{1+\tau s},
    30	\qquad
    31	S_i(s)=1+\frac{\sigma_i}{s},\quad i=x,y.
    32	\]
    33	In the physical region \(\sigma_x=\sigma_y=0\).  In the PML the coefficients are
    34	nonnegative and are first analyzed as piecewise constant near each planar
    35	interface.
    36	
    37	The Laplace-domain repaired model is
    38	\[
    39	\boxed{
    40	s\varepsilon_D(s)\widehat E
    41	=S_x^{-1}\partial_x\widehat H_y
    42	-S_y^{-1}\partial_y\widehat H_x,}
    43	\]
    44	\[
    45	\boxed{
    46	\mu s\widehat H_x=-S_y^{-1}\partial_y\widehat E,\qquad
    47	\mu s\widehat H_y=S_x^{-1}\partial_x\widehat E,}
    48	\]
    49	\[
    50	\boxed{(1+\tau s)\widehat P=\chi\widehat E.}
    51	\]
    52	Equivalently, the Debye law is not damped:
    53	\[
    54	P+\tau P_t=\chi E.
    55	\]
    56	
    57	### Perfect matching
    58	
    59	At an \(x\)-interface, \(S_y=1\).  With tangential Fourier number \(k_y\),
    60	the physical normal symbol satisfies
    61	\[
    62	\nu_0^2=k_y^2+\mu s^2\varepsilon_D(s),\qquad
    63	Y_0=\frac{\nu_0}{\mu s}.
    64	\]
    65	In the PML,
    66	\[
    67	s\varepsilon_D E=S_x^{-1}\nu H_y-ik_yH_x,\qquad
    68	\mu sH_x=-ik_yE,\qquad
    69	\mu sH_y=S_x^{-1}\nu E.
    70	\]
    71	The dispersion relation gives
    72	\[
    73	\left(S_x^{-1}\nu\right)^2=k_y^2+\mu s^2\varepsilon_D(s),
    74	\]
    75	hence \(\nu=S_x\nu_0\) and
    76	\[
    77	Y_+=\frac{S_x^{-1}\nu}{\mu s}=\frac{\nu_0}{\mu s}=Y_0.
    78	\]
    79	Thus the planar-interface reflection coefficient is \(R=0\) for every
    80	\((s,k_y)\) in the Laplace half-plane.  The same argument applies to a
    81	\(y\)-interface with \(x,y\) interchanged.
    82	
    83	### Time-domain ADE realization
    84	
    85	Define the causal operator
    86	\[
    87	\mathcal A_i=S_i^{-1}=\frac{s}{s+\sigma_i}
    88	\]
    89	in the Laplace domain.  Equivalently,
    90	\[
    91	\mathcal A_i f=f+\psi_i,\qquad
    92	(\partial_t+\sigma_i)\psi_i=-\sigma_i f.
    93	\]
    94	Then a time-domain unsplit ADE form is
    95	\[
    96	\epsilon_0\epsilon_\infty E_t+P_t
    97	=\partial_xH_y-\partial_yH_x
    98	+\psi_{E,x}-\psi_{E,y},
    99	\]
   100	\[
   101	\mu H_{x,t}=-\partial_yE-\psi_{H_x,y},\qquad
   102	\mu H_{y,t}=\partial_xE+\psi_{H_y,x},
   103	\]
   104	\[
   105	P+\tau P_t=\chi E,
   106	\]
   107	with
   108	\[
   109	(\partial_t+\sigma_x)\psi_{E,x}=-\sigma_x\partial_xH_y,\qquad
   110	(\partial_t+\sigma_y)\psi_{E,y}=-\sigma_y\partial_yH_x,
   111	\]
   112	\[
   113	(\partial_t+\sigma_y)\psi_{H_x,y}=-\sigma_y\partial_yE,\qquad
   114	(\partial_t+\sigma_x)\psi_{H_y,x}=-\sigma_x\partial_xE.
   115	\]
   116	Interface conditions are continuity of the physical tangential traces.  For an
   117	\(x\)-interface these are \(E\) and \(H_y\).  The auxiliary variables vanish in the
   118	physical region and are initialized consistently with the causal convolution.
   119	
   120	### Naive energy calculation
   121	
   122	The natural physical Debye energy is
   123	\[
   124	\mathcal E_{\rm phys}
   125	=\frac12\int_\Omega
   126	\left(\epsilon_0\epsilon_\infty E^2+\mu H_x^2+\mu H_y^2+\chi^{-1}P^2\right)\,dxdy.
   127	\]
   128	It is positive because
   129	\(\epsilon_0,\epsilon_\infty,\mu,\chi>0\).  Using
   130	\[
   131	E P_t=\frac{1}{2\chi}\partial_t(P^2)+\frac{\tau}{\chi}P_t^2
   132	\]
   133	and the PEC boundary condition \(E=0\) on the outer boundary gives
   134	\[
   135	\frac{d}{dt}\mathcal E_{\rm phys}
   136	=-\int_\Omega\frac{\tau}{\chi}P_t^2\,dxdy
   137	+\int_\Omega
   138	\left[
   139	E(\psi_{E,x}-\psi_{E,y})
   140	-H_x\psi_{H_x,y}
   141	+H_y\psi_{H_y,x}
   142	\right]\,dxdy .
   143	\]
   144	The Maxwell principal part contributes only the boundary flux
   145	\[
   146	\int_{\partial\Omega}E(H_y n_x-H_x n_y)\,ds,
   147	\]
   148	which vanishes under PEC at the outer boundary and cancels by transmission at
   149	internal material/PML interfaces when the tangential traces are continuous.
   150	
   151	The remaining auxiliary terms are not sign-definite in this naive energy.
   152	Therefore the positive physical Debye energy alone is not a monotone energy for
   153	the exact stretched-coordinate PML.
   154	
   155	### Classification
   156	
   157	This candidate is the formula-level perfect-matching repair.  A local monotone
   158	energy for the full 2D Maxwell--Debye ADE system is not certified here.  The
   159	calculation above identifies the exact terms that a Baffet-type augmented energy
   160	would have to absorb:
   161	\[
   162	E\psi_{E,x},\quad E\psi_{E,y},\quad
   163	H_x\psi_{H_x,y},\quad H_y\psi_{H_y,x}.
   164	\]
   165	The literature record supports that such augmented energies are non-naive and
   166	that constant-coefficient damping is the natural first scope for a sharp identity.
   167	
   168	### Reduced normal-incidence 1D energy identity
   169	
   170	There is one important positive result for the exact stretched-coordinate model.
   171	In the \(x\)-layer normal-incidence block \(k_y=0\), the standard stretch gives
   172	\[
   173	(\partial_t+\rho)(\epsilon_0\epsilon_\infty E+P)=\partial_xH_y,
   174	\qquad
   175	\mu(\partial_t+\rho)H_y=\partial_xE,
   176	\]
   177	\[
   178	P+\tau P_t=\chi E.
   179	\]
   180	This is exactly the \(k_y=0\) restriction of the perfectly matched stretched
   181	model, not the v2 model, because the Debye law still uses \(\partial_t\) rather
   182	than \(\partial_t+\rho\).
   183	
   184	Multiply the first equation by \(E\), the second by \(H_y\), and use
   185	\[
   186	E=\frac{P+\tau P_t}{\chi}.
   187	\]
   188	Then
   189	\[
   190	E P_t=\frac{1}{2\chi}\partial_t(P^2)+\frac{\tau}{\chi}P_t^2,
   191	\]
   192	and
   193	\[
   194	\rho E P
   195	=\frac{\rho}{\chi}P^2+\frac{\rho\tau}{2\chi}\partial_t(P^2).
   196	\]
   197	After integrating by parts, the principal terms give only the boundary flux
   198	\(\int_{\partial I}EH_y n_x\,ds\).  Hence
   199	\[
   200	\boxed{
   201	\frac{d}{dt}\mathcal E_{1d,sc}
   202	=-\int_I\left(
   203	\rho\epsilon_0\epsilon_\infty E^2+\mu\rho H_y^2
   204	+\frac{\rho}{\chi}P^2+\frac{\tau}{\chi}P_t^2
   205	\right)\,dx
   206	+\int_{\partial I}EH_y n_x\,ds,}
   207	\]
   208	where
   209	\[
   210	\boxed{
   211	\mathcal E_{1d,sc}
   212	=\frac12\int_I\left(
   213	\epsilon_0\epsilon_\infty E^2+\mu H_y^2
   214	+\frac{1+\rho\tau}{\chi}P^2
   215	\right)\,dx.}
   216	\]
   217	This energy is positive for \(\rho,\tau,\chi>0\), and it is dissipative under
   218	PEC or otherwise nonpositive boundary flux.  It explains why the v2 idea is
   219	close to a useful construction in normal incidence, but it does not solve the
   220	full 2D oblique problem: as soon as \(k_y\ne0\), the exact stretched model
   221	contains the ADE memory couplings displayed above.
   222	
   223	## Candidate 2: generalized CFS/ADE stretched-coordinate PML
   224	
   225	Let
   226	\[
   227	S_i(s)=\kappa_i+\frac{\sigma_i}{s+\alpha_i},
   228	\qquad
   229	\kappa_i\ge1,\quad \sigma_i\ge0,\quad \alpha_i\ge0.
   230	\]
   231	The repaired Laplace-domain equations are the same as Candidate 1, with these
   232	\(S_i\).  In particular the Debye law remains
   233	\[
   234	(1+\tau s)\widehat P=\chi\widehat E.
   235	\]
   236	
   237	For a planar \(x\)-interface with \(S_y=1\), the same calculation gives
   238	\[
   239	\nu=S_x\nu_0,\qquad Y_+=Y_0,
   240	\]
   241	so the continuous model is perfectly matched whenever the stretch is applied to
   242	the spatial derivatives and the physical material law is left unchanged.
   243	
   244	If \(S_i^{-1}\) is rational with poles in \(\Re s<0\), it can be implemented by
   245	ADE variables.  The CFS shift \(\alpha_i>0\) is a standard way to improve
   246	low-frequency/evanescent and late-time behavior, but a monotone time-domain
   247	energy requires an explicit positive realization of the memory kernel.  No such
   248	positive memory theorem is claimed here for the full 2D Maxwell--Debye system.
   249	
   250	Classification: perfectly matched at the continuous planar-interface level;
   251	recommended if long-time CFS behavior is needed; energy status is boundedness or
   252	passive-memory proof pending, not a completed monotone identity.
   253	
   254	## Candidate 3: MPML-type extra damping
   255	
   256	An MPML-type repair adds damping in more than the normal coordinate direction.
   257	For example, in an \(x\)-layer one may replace a scalar stretch by a multiaxial
   258	stretch depending also on tangential damping parameters.  This is useful for
   259	removing long-time instabilities or Jordan-block behavior in some systems.
   260	
   261	However, if the tangential stretch is nontrivial at the physical/PML interface,
   262	the planar admittance generally changes.  The MPML literature inspected for this
   263	run explicitly treats MPML as a stability-oriented absorbing layer and records
   264	that exact perfect matching may be lost in multiaxial variants.
   265	
   266	Classification: absorbing/stability repair, not the primary exact-matching
   267	repair for the present Maxwell--Debye interface theorem.
   268	
   269	## Complete dissipative identity that is currently verified
   270	
   271	The only complete positive monotone identity verified in the existing Iteris
   272	memory is for the v2 covariantly damped absorbing layer:
   273	\[
   274	\epsilon_0\epsilon_\infty D_\rho E
   275	=\partial_xH_y-\partial_yH_x-D_\rho P,
   276	\]
   277	\[
   278	\mu(\partial_t+\rho_y)H_x=-\partial_yE,\qquad
   279	\mu(\partial_t+\rho_x)H_y=\partial_xE,
   280	\]
   281	\[
   282	P+\tau D_\rho P=\chi E,\qquad D_\rho=\partial_t+\rho_x+\rho_y.
   283	\]
   284	Its energy is
   285	\[
   286	\mathcal E_\rho(t)=\frac12\int_\Omega
   287	\left(\epsilon_0\epsilon_\infty E^2+\mu H_x^2+\mu H_y^2+\chi^{-1}P^2\right)\,dxdy
   288	\]
   289	and the verified identity is
   290	\[
   291	\frac{d}{dt}\mathcal E_\rho(t)
   292	=-\int_\Omega\left(
   293	\epsilon_0\epsilon_\infty\rho E^2
   294	+\mu\rho_yH_x^2
   295	+\mu\rho_xH_y^2
   296	+\frac{\rho}{\chi}P^2
   297	+\frac{\tau}{\chi}|D_\rho P|^2
   298	\right)\,dxdy.
   299	\]
   300	This identity is genuinely dissipative, but the model is not perfectly matched.
   301	It should therefore be described as a stable absorbing-layer model, not as a
   302	standard PML.
   303	
   304	## Formula-level obstruction to strict decay on the whole domain
   305	
   306	Even for a perfectly matched repair, strict decay of a total energy controlling
   307	all fields on the whole computational domain cannot hold without a nullspace.
   308	Assume a physical subregion where \(\sigma_x=\sigma_y=0\) and choose
   309	\[
   310	E=0,\qquad P=0,\qquad H_x=\partial_x\phi,\qquad H_y=\partial_y\phi,
   311	\]
   312	with \(\phi\) smooth and compactly supported inside that undamped physical
   313	subregion.  Then
   314	\[
   315	\partial_xH_y-\partial_yH_x=0,\qquad
   316	\partial_yE=\partial_xE=0,
   317	\]
   318	and all PML auxiliary variables initialized at zero remain zero for at least this
   319	exact stationary solution.  The magnetic energy is positive if \(\nabla\phi\ne0\),
   320	but every damping term in the PML vanishes.

1	# Stage-3 proof: perfect-matching test for the v2 covariantly damped model
     2	
     3	Problem id: `2d_maxwell_pml_energy_functional_exploration`
     4	
     5	Task: `task-stage3-perfect-matching-test`
     6	
     7	## Assumptions and notation
     8	
     9	Use the alpha \(=1\) Maxwell--Debye material law in the physical region:
    10	\[
    11	P+\tau \partial_t P=\chi E,\qquad
    12	\varepsilon_D(s)=\epsilon_0\epsilon_\infty+\frac{\chi}{1+\tau s}.
    13	\]
    14	Here \(s\in\mathbb C\), \(\Re s>0\), is the Laplace frequency, and all initial
    15	data are taken zero for the interface symbol calculation.
    16	
    17	Consider a planar interface \(x=0\).  The physical half-space is \(x<0\).
    18	The PML half-space is \(x>0\), with constant \(x\)-layer coefficient
    19	\[
    20	\rho_x=\rho>0,\qquad \rho_y=0 .
    21	\]
    22	Use the tangential Fourier ansatz \(e^{s t+i k y+\nu x}\), so
    23	\(\partial_y\mapsto i k\), \(\partial_x\mapsto \nu\).  The square-root branch is
    24	chosen by outgoing/decaying continuation from \(\Re s>0\).
    25	
    26	For an \(x\)-interface the continuous tangential traces are \(E\) and \(H_y\).
    27	For incident and reflected physical modes,
    28	\[
    29	E=E_i+E_r,\qquad H_y=Y_0(E_i-E_r),
    30	\]
    31	and for the transmitted PML mode \(H_y=Y_+E_t\).  Hence
    32	\[
    33	R=\frac{E_r}{E_i}=\frac{Y_0-Y_+}{Y_0+Y_+}.
    34	\]
    35	The model is perfectly matched at this interface iff \(Y_+=Y_0\) for every
    36	\(s\) and \(k\).
    37	
    38	## Physical Maxwell--Debye admittance
    39	
    40	The Laplace-domain physical equations are
    41	\[
    42	s\varepsilon_D(s)E=\partial_xH_y-\partial_yH_x,
    43	\qquad
    44	\mu sH_x=-\partial_yE,\qquad
    45	\mu sH_y=\partial_xE .
    46	\]
    47	With \(\partial_x=\nu_0\), \(\partial_y=ik\),
    48	\[
    49	H_x=-\frac{ik}{\mu s}E,\qquad
    50	H_y=\frac{\nu_0}{\mu s}E .
    51	\]
    52	Substitution gives
    53	\[
    54	\nu_0^2=k^2+\mu s^2\varepsilon_D(s).
    55	\]
    56	Therefore the physical admittance is
    57	\[
    58	Y_0(s,k)=\frac{\nu_0}{\mu s},\qquad
    59	Y_0(s,k)^2=\frac{1}{\mu^2}\left(\mu\varepsilon_D(s)+\frac{k^2}{s^2}\right).
    60	\]
    61	
    62	## Standard stretched-coordinate check
    63	
    64	A classical \(x\)-PML has stretch factor
    65	\[
    66	S_x(s)=1+\frac{\sigma_x}{s}
    67	\]
    68	and replaces \(\partial_x\) by \(S_x^{-1}\partial_x\), while leaving the
    69	physical material law \(\varepsilon_D(s)\) unchanged:
    70	\[
    71	s\varepsilon_D(s)E=S_x^{-1}\partial_xH_y-\partial_yH_x,
    72	\quad
    73	\mu sH_x=-\partial_yE,\quad
    74	\mu sH_y=S_x^{-1}\partial_xE.
    75	\]
    76	For a transmitted mode,
    77	\[
    78	\nu_+=S_x\nu_0,\qquad
    79	Y_+=\frac{S_x^{-1}\nu_+}{\mu s}=\frac{\nu_0}{\mu s}=Y_0.
    80	\]
    81	Thus the stretched-coordinate model has \(R=0\) at the continuous planar
    82	interface.
    83	
    84	## v2 covariantly damped model
    85	
    86	The v2 model is
    87	\[
    88	\epsilon_0\epsilon_\infty D_\rho E
    89	=\partial_xH_y-\partial_yH_x-D_\rho P,
    90	\]
    91	\[
    92	\mu(\partial_t+\rho_y)H_x=-\partial_yE,\qquad
    93	\mu(\partial_t+\rho_x)H_y=\partial_xE,
    94	\]
    95	\[
    96	P+\tau D_\rho P=\chi E,\qquad
    97	D_\rho=\partial_t+\rho_x+\rho_y.
    98	\]
    99	In the \(x\)-layer \(\rho_x=\rho,\rho_y=0\), so
   100	\[
   101	P=\frac{\chi}{1+\tau(s+\rho)}E,\qquad
   102	\varepsilon_\rho(s)=
   103	\epsilon_0\epsilon_\infty+\frac{\chi}{1+\tau(s+\rho)} .
   104	\]
   105	The transformed equations are
   106	\[
   107	(s+\rho)\varepsilon_\rho(s)E=\nu H_y-ikH_x,
   108	\]
   109	\[
   110	\mu sH_x=-ikE,\qquad
   111	\mu(s+\rho)H_y=\nu E.
   112	\]
   113	Thus
   114	\[
   115	H_x=-\frac{ik}{\mu s}E,\qquad
   116	H_y=\frac{\nu}{\mu(s+\rho)}E
   117	\]
   118	and
   119	\[
   120	\nu^2=\mu(s+\rho)^2\varepsilon_\rho(s)
   121	      +k^2\frac{s+\rho}{s}.
   122	\]
   123	The v2 PML admittance is therefore
   124	\[
   125	Y_{v2}(s,k)=\frac{\nu}{\mu(s+\rho)},\qquad
   126	Y_{v2}(s,k)^2
   127	=\frac{1}{\mu^2}
   128	\left(\mu\varepsilon_\rho(s)+\frac{k^2}{s(s+\rho)}\right).
   129	\]
   130	
   131	Comparing with the physical admittance,
   132	\[
   133	Y_{v2}^2-Y_0^2
   134	=\frac{1}{\mu^2}\left[
   135	\mu(\varepsilon_\rho(s)-\varepsilon_D(s))
   136	+\frac{k^2}{s(s+\rho)}-\frac{k^2}{s^2}\right].
   137	\]
   138	Since
   139	\[
   140	\varepsilon_\rho(s)-\varepsilon_D(s)
   141	=-\frac{\chi\tau\rho}{(1+\tau s)(1+\tau(s+\rho))}
   142	\]
   143	and
   144	\[
   145	\frac{1}{s(s+\rho)}-\frac{1}{s^2}
   146	=-\frac{\rho}{s^2(s+\rho)},
   147	\]
   148	the exact mismatch is
   149	\[
   150	\boxed{
   151	Y_{v2}^2-Y_0^2
   152	=-\frac{\rho}{\mu^2}\left[
   153	\frac{\mu\chi\tau}{(1+\tau s)(1+\tau(s+\rho))}
   154	+\frac{k^2}{s^2(s+\rho)}
   155	\right].}
   156	\]
   157	This expression is not identically zero for \(\rho>0\).  Hence the v2 model is
   158	not perfectly matched.
   159	
   160	The corresponding reflection coefficient is
   161	\[
   162	\boxed{
   163	R_{v2}(s,k)=
   164	\frac{
   165	\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon_D(s)+k^2/s^2}
   166	-\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon_\rho(s)+k^2/[s(s+\rho)]}
   167	}{
   168	\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon_D(s)+k^2/s^2}
   169	+\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon_\rho(s)+k^2/[s(s+\rho)]}
   170	}.}
   171	\]
   172	The square-root branches are those inherited from the outgoing physical and
   173	decaying PML modes.
   174	
   175	## Interpretation of the mismatch
   176	
   177	There are two independent formula-level defects.
   178	
   179	1. The Debye susceptibility is shifted from
   180	\[
   181	\frac{\chi}{1+\tau s}
   182	\quad\text{to}\quad
   183	\frac{\chi}{1+\tau(s+\rho)}.
   184	\]
   185	This changes the material impedance even at normal incidence \(k=0\), unless
   186	\(\chi=0\), \(\tau=0\), or \(\rho=0\).
   187	
   188	2. The oblique tangential part changes from \(k^2/s^2\) to
   189	\[
   190	\frac{k^2}{s(s+\rho)}.
   191	\]
   192	This remains a mismatch for \(k\ne0\) even in the nondispersive limit
   193	\(\chi=0\).
   194	
   195	Thus applying the same covariant derivative \(D_\rho\) to the Debye law is good
   196	for the v2 monotone energy identity, but it is not the Laplace-domain
   197	stretched-coordinate continuation of the physical Maxwell--Debye system.
   198	
   199	## Durable fact candidate
   200	
   201	Claim summary:
   202	The covariantly damped v2 Maxwell--Debye absorbing-layer model is not perfectly
   203	matched at a planar constant-coefficient \(x\)-PML interface; its squared
   204	admittance differs from the physical Maxwell--Debye admittance by the boxed
   205	formula above.
   206	
   207	Dependencies:
   208	
   209	- `fact:2d_maxwell_pml_energy_functional_exploration:covariantly-damped-debye-energy`
   210	  for the v2 model definition and verified energy identity.

It compares three repairs:\n\n1. a compatibility restriction on the old auxiliary data;\n2. a shifted-variable MPML-style damping of the free magnetic auxiliary mode;\n3. a covariantly damped Maxwell-Debye absorbing-layer model.\n\nThe third model is the strongest fully closed result below: it has a positive\nmonotone energy identity for arbitrary data in its variables.  It is a modified\nabsorbing model, not algebraically identical to the old eight-variable unsplit\nPML formulation.\n\nThroughout this artifact\n\\[\n\\chi=\\epsilon_0(\\epsilon_s-\\epsilon_\\infty)>0,\\qquad\nb_x=\\frac{\\sigma_x}{\\epsilon_0},\\quad b_y=\\frac{\\sigma_y}{\\epsilon_0},\n\\]\nand\n\\[\na_x=\\frac{\\sigma_y-\\sigma_x}{\\epsilon_0}=b_y-b_x,\\qquad\na_y=\\frac{\\sigma_x-\\sigma_y}{\\epsilon_0}=b_x-b_y.\n\\]\n\n## Old-model obstruction term\n\nFor the source equations the shifted magnetic variables\n\\[\nM_x=Q_x-\\mu a_xH_x,\\qquad M_y=Q_y-\\mu a_yH_y\n\\]\nsatisfy\n\\[\nM_{x,t}=a_x\\partial_yE-b_yM_x,\\qquad\nM_{y,t}=-a_y\\partial_xE-b_xM_y .\n\\]\nIn the \\(x\\)-edge case \\(\\sigma_x=s>0,\\sigma_y=0\\), the spatially constant\nmode with\n\\[\nE=P=P_{z,1}=P_{z,2}=H_y=Q_y=0\n\\]\nhas \\(M_x=Q_x+\\mu b_xH_x\\) conserved.  Hence\n\\[\nH_x(t)=H_x(0)+\\frac{M_x(0)}{\\mu}t,\\qquad\nQ_x(t)=Q_x(0)-b_xM_x(0)t .\n\\]\nThe obstruction is therefore the undamped shifted magnetic auxiliary \\(M_x\\) in\nthe edge direction with zero transverse damping.  The \\(y\\)-edge case is\nsymmetric with \\(M_y\\).\n\n## Repair 1: compatibility restriction on old auxiliaries\n\nThe weakest repair is to restrict the old model to a physical auxiliary\nsubspace that excludes the verified free mode.  In the constant \\(x\\)-edge\ncase this means\n\\[\nM_x(0)=Q_x(0)+\\mu b_xH_x(0)=0\n\\]\nfor the spatially constant edge mode; in the constant \\(y\\)-edge case it means\n\\[\nM_y(0)=Q_y(0)+\\mu b_yH_y(0)=0 .\n\\]\nThis compatibility condition is physically meaningful if the old \\(Q\\)\nvariables are interpreted as derived PML histories rather than independent\ninitial data.\n\nThe candidate energy for this restricted old model remains the positive\naugmented source energy\n\\[\n\\mathcal E_0(t)\n=\\frac12\\int_\\Omega\\left(\n\\epsilon_0\\epsilon_\\infty E^2+\\mu H_x^2+\\mu H_y^2\n+\\chi^{-1}P^2+P_{z,1}^2+P_{z,2}^2+Q_x^2+Q_y^2\n\\right)\\,dxdy .\n\\]\nUnder only bounded nonnegative absorptions, the previous verified result gives\n\\[\n\\mathcal E_0'(t)\\le C_G\\mathcal E_0(t).\n\\]\nThe compatibility condition removes the exact linear edge mode in the\none-dimensional constant-mode test.  It does not by itself give a closed\ntwo-dimensional monotone energy, because in an \\(x\\)-edge\n\\[\nM_{x,t}=-b_x\\partial_yE\n\\]\nwhen \\(\\sigma_y=0\\). Classification: useful compatibility repair for\nthe old edge free mode, but not a complete 2D monotone repair.\n\n## Repair 2: shifted-variable MPML damping\n\nThe second repair keeps the shifted magnetic variables but adds a multi-axial\nor CFS-style damping \\(\\eta_x,\\eta_y\\ge0\\) to the modes that were undamped at\nedges.  The modified \\(Q\\) equations are\n\\[\nQ_{x,t}=-(b_x+\\eta_x)Q_x+\\mu(b_x+\\eta_x)a_xH_x,\n\\]\n\\[\nQ_{y,t}=-(b_y+\\eta_y)Q_y+\\mu(b_y+\\eta_y)a_yH_y,\n\\]\nwhile the \\(E,H,P,P_z\\) equations are unchanged.  Equivalently,\n\\[\nM_{x,t}=a_x\\partial_yE-(b_y+\\eta_x)M_x,\n\\qquad\nM_{y,t}=-a_y\\partial_xE-(b_x+\\eta_y)M_y .\n\\]\nThus the old \\(x\\)-edge constant-mode obstruction becomes\n\\[\nH_{x,t}=\\frac{M_x}{\\mu},\\qquad M_{x,t}=-\\eta_x M_x\n\\]\nwhen \\(E=0\\), \\(\\sigma_x>0\\), and \\(\\sigma_y=0\\).  If \\(\\eta_x>0\\), then for any\nconstant \\(c_x>0\\)\n\\[\n\\mathcal E_{x,\\eta}\n=\\frac{\\mu}{2}\\left|H_x+\\frac{M_x}{\\mu\\eta_x}\\right|^2\n+\\frac{c_x}{2}|M_x|^2\n\\]\nis positive in \\((H_x,M_x)\\) and satisfies\n\\[\n\\frac{d}{dt}\\mathcal E_{x,\\eta}=-c_x\\eta_x|M_x|^2\\le0 .\n\\]\nThe \\(y\\)-edge formula is identical with \\(x\\) and \\(y\\) interchanged.\n\nThis repair removes the specific linear-growth obstruction without imposing\nthe compatibility \\(M_i(0)=0\\).  In the full two-dimensional system the energy\nderivative still contains transverse derivative couplings\n\\[\nM_x\\partial_yE,\\qquad M_y\\partial_xE,\n\\]\nso a purely zeroth-order monotone energy is not closed by this shift alone.\nWith derivative energies these terms are candidates for a dissipative\nlower-order or Gronwall estimate.  Classification: monotone for the isolated\nedge free subsystem, promising MPML repair for the old obstruction, but not a\ncompleted full 2D monotone proof in this artifact.\n\n## Repair 3: covariantly damped Maxwell-Debye absorbing layer\n\nThe best closed repair is to replace the old independent \\(P_z,Q\\) auxiliary\nsystem by a covariantly damped Maxwell-Debye absorbing layer.  Let\n\\(\\rho_x,\\rho_y\\in L^\\infty(\\Omega)\\) be nonnegative, time-independent layer\nprofiles that vanish in the physical region, and put\n\\[\n\\rho=\\rho_x+\\rho_y,\\qquad D_\\rho=\\partial_t+\\rho .\n\\]\nThe modified model is\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\epsilon_0\\epsilon_\\infty D_\\rho E\n&=\\partial_xH_y-\\partial_yH_x-D_\\rho P,\\\\\n\\mu(\\partial_t+\\rho_y)H_x&=-\\partial_yE,\\\\\n\\mu(\\partial_t+\\rho_x)H_y&=\\partial_xE,\\\\\nP+\\tau D_\\rho P&=\\chi E .\n\\end{aligned}}\n\\]\nThe boundary condition is the same PEC condition,\n\\[\nE=0\\quad\\text{on }\\partial\\Omega .\n\\]\n\nThe model is local, agrees with the physical alpha \\(=1\\) Maxwell-Debye system\nwhere \\(\\rho_x=\\rho_y=0\\), and damps the electric polarization by the same\ncovariant derivative used in the layer equation.  This last point is the\nessential repair of the old source-model term\n\\(-((\\sigma_x+\\sigma_y)/\\epsilon_0)EP\\): the damping is applied to the\nDebye law itself, so the polarization contribution becomes positive\ndissipation rather than a sign-indefinite mixed product.\n\n### Candidate energy and positivity\n\nUse\n\\[\n\\mathcal E_\\rho(t)\n=\\frac12\\int_\\Omega\\left(\n\\epsilon_0\\epsilon_\\infty E^2+\\mu H_x^2+\\mu H_y^2+\\chi^{-1}P^2\n\\right)\\,dxdy .\n\\]\nThis energy is positive definite in \\((E,H_x,H_y,P)\\) because\n\\(\\epsilon_0,\\epsilon_\\infty,\\mu,\\chi>0\\).\n\n### Energy identity\n\nMultiplying the electric equation by \\(E\\), the magnetic equations by\n\\(H_x,H_y\\), integrating over \\(\\Omega\\), and using \\(E=0\\) on\n\\(\\partial\\Omega\\) gives cancellation of the Maxwell principal boundary flux:\n\\[\n\\int_\\Omega\n\\left(E\\partial_xH_y-E\\partial_yH_x-H_x\\partial_yE+H_y\\partial_xE\\right)\n\\,dxdy=0 .\n\\]\nThe covariant polarization law gives\n\\[\nE\\,D_\\rho P\n=\\frac{1}{\\chi}P\\,D_\\rho P+\\frac{\\tau}{\\chi}|D_\\rho P|^2\n=\\frac{1}{2\\chi}\\partial_t(P^2)\n+\\frac{\\rho}{\\chi}P^2\n+\\frac{\\tau}{\\chi}|D_\\rho P|^2 .\n\\]\nTherefore\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{d}{dt}\\mathcal E_\\rho(t)\n=-\\int_\\Omega\\left(\n\\epsilon_0\\epsilon_\\infty\\rho E^2\n+\\mu\\rho_yH_x^2\n+\\mu\\rho_xH_y^2\n+\\frac{\\rho}{\\chi}P^2\n+\\frac{\\tau}{\\chi}|D_\\rho P|^2\n\\right)\\,dxdy\\le0 .}\n\\]\n\nConsequently\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\mathcal E_\\rho(t)\\le \\mathcal E_\\rho(0)\\quad\\text{for all }t\\ge0.}\n\\]\nThis is a genuinely monotone, long-time-uniform energy estimate.  It contains\nno independent \\(P_{z,i}\\) or \\(Q_i\\) variables, so the old edge free mode is\nnot present.\n\n### Absorbing-layer status\n\nThis repair should be viewed as a certified stable absorbing Maxwell-Debye\nlayer.  It is PML-like in the sense that the layer profiles vanish in the\nphysical region and the layer applies directional magnetic damping\n\\(\\rho_y,\\rho_x\\) together with covariant electric-polarization damping\n\\(\\rho=\\rho_x+\\rho_y\\).  The proof above establishes stability and absorption\nthrough a monotone energy.  It does not prove exact perfect matching for every\nincidence angle; if exact reflectionless matching is required, a separate\nfrequency-domain matching calculation remains open.\n\n## Selection\n\nThe compatibility repair is too narrow for a full 2D theorem.  The MPML shift\ndirectly repairs the verified edge free mode, but its full 2D monotone energy\nrequires additional derivative or nonlocal structure.\n\nThe covariantly damped Maxwell-Debye absorbing layer is the selected best\ncandidate because it has a closed positive energy and an exact monotone\nidentity under variable nonnegative layer profiles.  Its limitation is that it\nis a modified absorbing model rather than a proof that the old eight-variable\nunsplit PML has a monotone energy.\n","exit_code":0,"status":"completed"}}
verification/agent_runs/verify-20260620T023007094217Z-assembly-assemble-verified-facts-to-answ/codex.events.jsonl:32:{"type":"item.completed","item":{"id":"item_14","type":"command_execution","command":"/bin/zsh -lc \"sed -n '1,260p' sources/energy_functional_problem.tex\"","aggregated_output":"\\documentclass[UTF8,a4paper,12pt]{ctexart}\n\\input{macros}\n\n\\title{Problem Sheet for Iteris: Energy Functionals for 2D Maxwell--PML}\n\\author{Prepared source problem}\n\\date{\\today}\n\n\\begin{document}\n\\maketitle\n\n\\begin{abstract}\nThis note is a self-contained source problem for an Iteris run.  The system to be analyzed is the two-dimensional TM Maxwell--PML model with polarization \\(P\\), PML auxiliary variables \\(P_{z,1},P_{z,2},Q_x,Q_y\\), and perfectly conducting boundary condition.  The first target is to find a genuinely monotone decreasing energy functional in two space dimensions.  If such a monotone energy cannot be found, the fallback target is to find a positive energy functional that proves boundedness/no abnormal long-time growth, in the same spirit as the long-time-stability role of MPML.  The non-fractional case should be understood as the special case \\(\\alpha=1\\) of the displayed polarization law.\n\\end{abstract}\n\n\\section{Primary Goal}\n\nLet \\(\\Om\\subset\\R^2\\) be a rectangular computational domain containing a physical region and a PML layer.  The absorption parameters are\n\\[\n  \\sx=\\sx(x)\\ge0,\\qquad \\sy=\\sy(y)\\ge0,\n\\]\nor, in a harder variant,\n\\[\n  \\sx=\\sx(x,y)\\ge0,\\qquad \\sy=\\sy(x,y)\\ge0.\n\\]\nThe main goal is to analyze the two-dimensional system in Section~\\ref{sec:model} and construct an energy functional \\(\\Ecal(t)\\).\n\n\\begin{enumerate}\n\\item \\textbf{Strong target: monotone decreasing energy.}\nFind a positive energy functional such that\n\\[\n  \\frac{\\dd}{\\dd t}\\Ecal(t)=-\\Dcal(t)\\le0.\n\\]\nThis is the preferred outcome.\n\\item \\textbf{Fallback target: bounded/non-growing energy.}\nIf no monotone energy can be found, find a positive energy functional that rules out abnormal growth from the PML layer, for example\n\\[\n  \\Ecal(t)\\le C\\,\\Ecal(0)\n\\]\nwith \\(C\\) independent of long time if possible.  If only a Gronwall estimate\n\\[\n  \\frac{\\dd}{\\dd t}\\Ecal(t)\\le C_\\sigma\\Ecal(t)\n\\]\nis available, identify the precise terms responsible for the possible growth and whether they are coefficient-gradient terms, corner-PML terms, or algebraic sign-indefinite terms.\n\\item \\textbf{Useful obstruction.}\nIf the strong target fails for natural quadratic energies, prove or at least sharply identify the obstruction.  An obstruction result is valuable if it explains which part of the PML coupling prevents monotonicity.\n\\end{enumerate}\n\nThe energy may include weighted \\(L^2\\) norms, cross terms, shifted variables, time-integrated auxiliary variables, polarization energy, fractional-memory energy, and derivative terms if they are mathematically justified.\n\n\\section{Model to Analyze}\n\\label{sec:model}\n\nThe model is the system shown in the supplied manuscript image.  Write\n\\[\n  E=E_z,\\qquad \\epsilon_\\infty=\\epsilon_{r,\\infty},\\qquad\n  \\epsilon_s=\\epsilon_{r,s},\\qquad \\mu=\\mu_0\\mu_r,\n\\]\nand\n\\[\n  \\chi=\\epsilon_0(\\epsilon_s-\\epsilon_\\infty).\n\\]\nThe unknowns are\n\\[\n  E,\\quad H_x,\\quad H_y,\\quad P,\\quad P_{z,1},\\quad P_{z,2},\\quad Q_x,\\quad Q_y.\n\\]\nThe PML system is\n\\begin{equation}\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\epsilon_0\\epsilon_\\infty\\,\\partial_t E\n&= \\partial_xH_y-\\partial_yH_x\n   -\\epsilon_\\infty(\\sx+\\sy)E\n   -\\partial_tP-\\frac{\\sx+\\sy}{\\epsilon_0}P\n   +P_{z,1}+P_{z,2},\\\\\n\\mu\\,\\partial_tH_x\n&= -\\partial_yE-\\mu\\frac{\\sy-\\sx}{\\epsilon_0}H_x+Q_x,\\\\\n\\mu\\,\\partial_tH_y\n&= \\partial_xE-\\mu\\frac{\\sx-\\sy}{\\epsilon_0}H_y+Q_y,\\\\\nP+\\tau^\\alpha\\partial_t^\\alpha P\n&=\\chi E,\\\\\n\\partial_tP_{z,1}\n&=-\\frac{\\epsilon_\\infty}{\\epsilon_0}\\sx\\sy E,\\\\\n\\partial_tP_{z,2}\n&=-\\frac{\\sx\\sy}{\\epsilon_0^2}P,\\\\\n\\partial_tQ_x\n&=-\\frac{\\sx}{\\epsilon_0}Q_x\n  +\\frac{\\mu\\sx(\\sy-\\sx)}{\\epsilon_0^2}H_x,\\\\\n\\partial_tQ_y\n&=-\\frac{\\sy}{\\epsilon_0}Q_y\n  +\\frac{\\mu\\sy(\\sx-\\sy)}{\\epsilon_0^2}H_y.\n\\end{aligned}\n\\label{eq:main-model}\n\\end{equation}\nHere \\(\\partial_t^\\alpha\\) should be interpreted as a Caputo-type fractional derivative when \\(0<\\alpha<1\\).  The non-fractional case requested by the user is the case\n\\[\n  \\alpha=1,\\qquad\n  P+\\tau\\partial_tP=\\chi E.\n\\]\nThus the first stage of the analysis should use \\(\\alpha=1\\), not a model with \\(P\\) removed.\n\nThe boundary condition is the perfectly conducting boundary condition\n\\[\n  \\widehat n\\times E=0\\qquad\\text{on }\\partial\\Om.\n\\]\nFor the two-dimensional TM model this should be interpreted as\n\\[\n  E=E_z=0\\qquad\\text{on }\\partial\\Om,\n\\]\nso that the Maxwell principal part has no positive boundary contribution.  If a proof uses a different boundary condition, it must state that choice explicitly.\n\n\\begin{remark}\nThe parameters \\(\\epsilon_0,\\epsilon_\\infty,\\epsilon_s,\\mu,\\tau\\) are positive, and \\(\\chi>0\\) when \\(\\epsilon_s>\\epsilon_\\infty\\).  The absorption parameters are time-independent and nonnegative.  The first serious cases to analyze are constant \\(\\sx,\\sy\\), then separated variable coefficients \\(\\sx(x),\\sy(y)\\), and only then general \\(\\sx(x,y),\\sy(x,y)\\).\n\\end{remark}\n\n\\section{First Energy Balance to Verify}\n\nStart with the electromagnetic part\n\\[\n  \\Ecal_{\\rm em}(t)=\\frac12\\int_\\Om\n  \\left(\\epsilon_0\\epsilon_\\infty E^2+\\mu H_x^2+\\mu H_y^2\\right)\\dd x\\dd y.\n\\]\n\n\\begin{task}[Check the electromagnetic energy derivative]\nUsing \\eqref{eq:main-model} and the PEC boundary condition, verify that the Maxwell principal part cancels by integration by parts, and that\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\frac{\\dd}{\\dd t}\\Ecal_{\\rm em}\n=\\int_\\Om\\Big[\n&-\\epsilon_\\infty(\\sx+\\sy)E^2\n-E\\partial_tP\n-\\frac{\\sx+\\sy}{\\epsilon_0}EP\n+E(P_{z,1}+P_{z,2})\\\\\n&-\\frac{\\mu}{\\epsilon_0}(\\sy-\\sx)H_x^2\n-\\frac{\\mu}{\\epsilon_0}(\\sx-\\sy)H_y^2\n+H_xQ_x+H_yQ_y\n\\Big]\\dd x\\dd y .\n\\end{aligned}\n\\label{eq:em-balance}\n\\]\nThe terms involving \\(H_x,H_y\\) are sign-indefinite when \\(\\sx\\ne\\sy\\).  The terms involving \\(P,P_{z,1},P_{z,2}\\) are the electric/PML auxiliary coupling terms that must be absorbed by a refined energy.\n\\end{task}\n\n\\section{The \\texorpdfstring{\\(\\alpha=1\\)}{alpha=1} Polarization Identity}\n\nFor the non-fractional case \\(\\alpha=1\\),\n\\[\n  P+\\tau\\partial_tP=\\chi E,\n\\]\nso\n\\[\n  E=\\frac{P+\\tau\\partial_tP}{\\chi}.\n\\]\nThis gives the useful identity\n\\begin{equation}\n  E\\,\\partial_tP\n  =\\frac{1}{2\\chi}\\frac{\\dd}{\\dd t}\\|P\\|_{L^2(\\Om)}^2\n   +\\frac{\\tau}{\\chi}\\|\\partial_tP\\|_{L^2(\\Om)}^2.\n\\label{eq:alpha-one-dissipation}\n\\end{equation}\n\n\\begin{task}[Use the alpha=1 identity]\nUse \\eqref{eq:alpha-one-dissipation} to decide whether the energy\n\\[\n  \\Ecal_{\\rm em+P}\n  =\\Ecal_{\\rm em}+\\frac{1}{2\\chi}\\|P\\|_{L^2(\\Om)}^2\n\\]\nis the right starting point.  Then identify the remaining troublesome electric auxiliary terms:\n\\[\n  -\\frac{\\sx+\\sy}{\\epsilon_0}EP,\\qquad\n  E P_{z,1},\\qquad\n  E P_{z,2},\\qquad\n  \\partial_tP_{z,1},\\qquad\n  \\partial_tP_{z,2}.\n\\]\nTry to absorb them using cross terms, shifted variables, or time-integrated variables.\n\\end{task}\n\n\\section{Magnetic Auxiliary Variable Shift}\n\nDefine\n\\[\n  a_x=\\frac{\\sy-\\sx}{\\epsilon_0},\\qquad\n  a_y=\\frac{\\sx-\\sy}{\\epsilon_0},\\qquad\n  b_x=\\frac{\\sx}{\\epsilon_0},\\qquad\n  b_y=\\frac{\\sy}{\\epsilon_0}.\n\\]\nThe magnetic equations and \\(Q_x,Q_y\\) equations suggest the shifted variables\n\\[\n  M_x=Q_x-\\mu a_xH_x,\\qquad\n  M_y=Q_y-\\mu a_yH_y.\n\\]\n\n\\begin{task}[Verify shifted magnetic identities]\nStarting from \\eqref{eq:main-model}, verify\n\\begin{equation}\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\partial_tM_x\n&= a_x\\,\\partial_yE-\\frac{\\sy}{\\epsilon_0}M_x,\\\\\n\\partial_tM_y\n&= -a_y\\,\\partial_xE-\\frac{\\sx}{\\epsilon_0}M_y.\n\\end{aligned}\n\\label{eq:magnetic-shift}\n\\end{equation}\nThen test whether an energy written in terms of \\(H_x,H_y,M_x,M_y\\), rather than \\(H_x,H_y,Q_x,Q_y\\), has a cleaner dissipation structure.\n\\end{task}\n\n\\begin{remark}\nIf \\(\\sx,\\sy\\) are spatially variable, \\eqref{eq:magnetic-shift} itself does not produce \\(\\partial_t\\sigma\\) terms, because the coefficients are time-independent.  However, integrated energy identities may produce \\(\\partial_x\\sx\\), \\(\\partial_y\\sy\\), or general \\(\\nabla\\sigma_i\\) terms after integration by parts.  These terms are likely to be one source of bounded-but-not-monotone estimates.\n\\end{remark}\n\n\\section{Electric PML Auxiliary Variables}\n\nThe variables \\(P_{z,1}\\) and \\(P_{z,2}\\) satisfy\n\\[\n  \\partial_tP_{z,1}=-\\frac{\\epsilon_\\infty}{\\epsilon_0}\\sx\\sy E,\\qquad\n  \\partial_tP_{z,2}=-\\frac{\\sx\\sy}{\\epsilon_0^2}P.\n\\]\nThey appear in the \\(E\\)-equation as \\(E(P_{z,1}+P_{z,2})\\). In an \\(x\\)-layer with \\(\\rho_x=\\rho>0,\\rho_y=0\\),\n    12\t\\[\n    13\tY_{v2}^2-Y_0^2\n    14\t=-\\frac{\\rho}{\\mu^2}\\left[\n    15\t\\frac{\\mu\\chi\\tau}{(1+\\tau s)(1+\\tau(s+\\rho))}\n    16\t+\\frac{k_y^2}{s^2(s+\\rho)}\n    17\t\\right],\n    18\t\\]\n    19\tso the v2 reflection coefficient is not identically zero.\n    20\t\n    21\tTherefore a repaired model must keep the physical Debye law as a function of the\n    22\tLaplace variable \\(s\\), not \\(s+\\rho\\), and must implement damping through\n    23\tcoordinate stretching or an equivalent split/ADE system.\n    24\t\n    25\t## Candidate 1: classical stretched-coordinate Maxwell--Debye PML\n    26\t\n    27\tLet\n    28\t\\[\n    29\t\\varepsilon_D(s)=\\epsilon_0\\epsilon_\\infty+\\frac{\\chi}{1+\\tau s},\n    30\t\\qquad\n    31\tS_i(s)=1+\\frac{\\sigma_i}{s},\\quad i=x,y.\n    32\t\\]\n    33\tIn the physical region \\(\\sigma_x=\\sigma_y=0\\).  In the PML the coefficients are\n    34\tnonnegative and are first analyzed as piecewise constant near each planar\n    35\tinterface.\n    36\t\n    37\tThe Laplace-domain repaired model is\n    38\t\\[\n    39\t\\boxed{\n    40\ts\\varepsilon_D(s)\\widehat E\n    41\t=S_x^{-1}\\partial_x\\widehat H_y\n    42\t-S_y^{-1}\\partial_y\\widehat H_x,}\n    43\t\\]\n    44\t\\[\n    45\t\\boxed{\n    46\t\\mu s\\widehat H_x=-S_y^{-1}\\partial_y\\widehat E,\\qquad\n    47\t\\mu s\\widehat H_y=S_x^{-1}\\partial_x\\widehat E,}\n    48\t\\]\n    49\t\\[\n    50\t\\boxed{(1+\\tau s)\\widehat P=\\chi\\widehat E.}\n    51\t\\]\n    52\tEquivalently, the Debye law is not damped:\n    53\t\\[\n    54\tP+\\tau P_t=\\chi E.\n    55\t\\]\n    56\t\n    57\t### Perfect matching\n    58\t\n    59\tAt an \\(x\\)-interface, \\(S_y=1\\). The same argument applies to a\n    81\t\\(y\\)-interface with \\(x,y\\) interchanged.\n    82\t\n    83\t### Time-domain ADE realization\n    84\t\n    85\tDefine the causal operator\n    86\t\\[\n    87\t\\mathcal A_i=S_i^{-1}=\\frac{s}{s+\\sigma_i}\n    88\t\\]\n    89\tin the Laplace domain.  Equivalently,\n    90\t\\[\n    91\t\\mathcal A_i f=f+\\psi_i,\\qquad\n    92\t(\\partial_t+\\sigma_i)\\psi_i=-\\sigma_i f.\n    93\t\\]\n    94\tThen a time-domain unsplit ADE form is\n    95\t\\[\n    96\t\\epsilon_0\\epsilon_\\infty E_t+P_t\n    97\t=\\partial_xH_y-\\partial_yH_x\n    98\t+\\psi_{E,x}-\\psi_{E,y},\n    99\t\\]\n   100\t\\[\n   101\t\\mu H_{x,t}=-\\partial_yE-\\psi_{H_x,y},\\qquad\n   102\t\\mu H_{y,t}=\\partial_xE+\\psi_{H_y,x},\n   103\t\\]\n   104\t\\[\n   105\tP+\\tau P_t=\\chi E,\n   106\t\\]\n   107\twith\n   108\t\\[\n   109\t(\\partial_t+\\sigma_x)\\psi_{E,x}=-\\sigma_x\\partial_xH_y,\\qquad\n   110\t(\\partial_t+\\sigma_y)\\psi_{E,y}=-\\sigma_y\\partial_yH_x,\n   111\t\\]\n   112\t\\[\n   113\t(\\partial_t+\\sigma_y)\\psi_{H_x,y}=-\\sigma_y\\partial_yE,\\qquad\n   114\t(\\partial_t+\\sigma_x)\\psi_{H_y,x}=-\\sigma_x\\partial_xE.\n   115\t\\]\n   116\tInterface conditions are continuity of the physical tangential traces.  For an\n   117\t\\(x\\)-interface these are \\(E\\) and \\(H_y\\).  The auxiliary variables vanish in the\n   118\tphysical region and are initialized consistently with the causal convolution.\n   119\t\n   120\t### Naive energy calculation\n   121\t\n   122\tThe natural physical Debye energy is\n   123\t\\[\n   124\t\\mathcal E_{\\rm phys}\n   125\t=\\frac12\\int_\\Omega\n   126\t\\left(\\epsilon_0\\epsilon_\\infty E^2+\\mu H_x^2+\\mu H_y^2+\\chi^{-1}P^2\\right)\\,dxdy.\n   127\t\\]\n   128\tIt is positive because\n   129\t\\(\\epsilon_0,\\epsilon_\\infty,\\mu,\\chi>0\\). The\n   159\tcalculation above identifies the exact terms that a Baffet-type augmented energy\n   160\twould have to absorb:\n   161\t\\[\n   162\tE\\psi_{E,x},\\quad E\\psi_{E,y},\\quad\n   163\tH_x\\psi_{H_x,y},\\quad H_y\\psi_{H_y,x}.\n   164\t\\]\n   165\tThe literature record supports that such augmented energies are non-naive and\n   166\tthat constant-coefficient damping is the natural first scope for a sharp identity.\n   167\t\n   168\t### Reduced normal-incidence 1D energy identity\n   169\t\n   170\tThere is one important positive result for the exact stretched-coordinate model.\n   171\tIn the \\(x\\)-layer normal-incidence block \\(k_y=0\\), the standard stretch gives\n   172\t\\[\n   173\t(\\partial_t+\\rho)(\\epsilon_0\\epsilon_\\infty E+P)=\\partial_xH_y,\n   174\t\\qquad\n   175\t\\mu(\\partial_t+\\rho)H_y=\\partial_xE,\n   176\t\\]\n   177\t\\[\n   178\tP+\\tau P_t=\\chi E.\n   179\t\\]\n   180\tThis is exactly the \\(k_y=0\\) restriction of the perfectly matched stretched\n   181\tmodel, not the v2 model, because the Debye law still uses \\(\\partial_t\\) rather\n   182\tthan \\(\\partial_t+\\rho\\).\n   183\t\n   184\tMultiply the first equation by \\(E\\), the second by \\(H_y\\), and use\n   185\t\\[\n   186\tE=\\frac{P+\\tau P_t}{\\chi}.\n   187\t\\]\n   188\tThen\n   189\t\\[\n   190\tE P_t=\\frac{1}{2\\chi}\\partial_t(P^2)+\\frac{\\tau}{\\chi}P_t^2,\n   191\t\\]\n   192\tand\n   193\t\\[\n   194\t\\rho E P\n   195\t=\\frac{\\rho}{\\chi}P^2+\\frac{\\rho\\tau}{2\\chi}\\partial_t(P^2).\n   196\t\\]\n   197\tAfter integrating by parts, the principal terms give only the boundary flux\n   198\t\\(\\int_{\\partial I}EH_y n_x\\,ds\\). AN ELEMENTARY INTRODUCTION TO THE CONSTRUCTION AND THE
ANALYSIS OF PERFECTLY MATCHED LAYERS FOR TIME DOMAIN
WAVE PROPAGATION

PATRICK JOLY

POEMS, UMR CNRS/ENSTA/INRIA
INRIA, Domaine de Voluceau-Rocquencourt, BP 105, F-78153 Le Chesnay C´edex

Patrick.Joly@inria.fr

As soon as people have been interested in the numerical simulation of wave propa-
gation phenomena, particularly in the time domain, they had to face the delicate ques-
tion of realizing “transparent” artiﬁcial boundaries. Indeed, many problems of this type
are posed in a unbounded domain (or in a domain which is very large with respect to
a zone of interest in which one wishes to observe the solution) : one thus has to bound
artiﬁcially the computational domain in such a way that the non physical boundaries
are “transparent” for the solution. Due to the crucial importance of this subject, but
also because of its difﬁculty, this question has aroused the curiosity from many re-
searchers, ﬁrst from engineers, next from applied mathematicians. It would be much
too ambitious to give a complete panorama of a research that began almost forty years
ago (see however the article by T. Hagstrm [20] which constitutes a quite complete
review of the domain) but one can now measure how much the many ingenious ideas
proposed by the one or the others have permitted to accomplish impressive progress
in this matter. Nowadays, if one restricts oneself to linear wave propagation problems,
one can consider that, even though some questions remain open, satisfactory solutions
are available for a large number of applications, in particular in the “canonical case” I
will have in mind throughout this paper, namely the case where one wishes to reduce
numerical computations to a convex bounded domain, assuming that the exterior do-
main is homogeneous and source free.

Recently, in particular for the applications in acoustics and electromagnetism, impor-
tant progress has been achieved in the use of “exact” boundary conditions associated
to homogeneous exterior domains. One usually introduces a boundary operator called
“Dirichlet to Neumann” (DtN) operator that can be represented by using separation of
variables in the exterior domain (in 3D, one will use typically spherical harmonics [19],
which requires a spherical artiﬁcial boundary) or through the coupling with an integral
representation formula of the exterior solution (which relies on the explicit knowledge
of the Green’s function of the problem) [4].

However, these techniques, beyond the fact that they remain restricted to a relatively
limited ﬁeld of applications, have the disadvantage to be nonlocal in space and time
: they remain quite difﬁcult to implement and rather costly in terms of computational
time and storage, despite of the recent progress accomplished is fast algorithms for the
evaluation of such nonlocal operators, such as the multipole method [18]. That is why,
in many computational codes, one prefers to use solutions involving local operators,
typically differential operators, which lead to a much simpler implementation. Such
solutions, except in 1D, can not provide transparent boundary conditions : one speaks
of ”approximate” or ”absorbing” boundary conditions. Of course, these conditions in-
volve approximation parameters (devoted to tend to 0 or +∞) and will provide the true
solution only when ”passing to the limit”. In this class of methods, two large families
of methods can be opposed:

• Absorbing boundary conditions (ABC’s): The idea is to complete the interior
mathematical model (namely the interior PDE’s) with one or several boundary
conditions that can be seen as partial differential equations along the boundary.
Such conditions are supposed to minimize the spurious reﬂections that they
generate. The pioneering works of Engquist and Majda [15], [16] on the wave
equation (in the half space, i. e. with a ﬂat artiﬁcial boundary) are in this spirit.
They proposed a hierarchy of boundary conditions that are classiﬁed with an
integer N , namely the order of the boundary condition that I will not precisely
deﬁne here. Let us simply explain that the greater is N , the higher is the order of
the differential operators (which means that the boundary condition is more and
more costly in terms of computational time) and the better is the accuracy of the
approximate solution, as it has been recently proven in [14] for instance. These
initial works have led to an intensive research in applied mathematics aiming
at extending this type of techniques to other equations, the treatment of curved
boundaries, the treatment of corners,...

• Absorbing layers : the idea here is that the absorption of the waves that ”want”
to leave the computational domain is not achieved through a boundary condition
but inside a (hopefully small) layer surrounding this computational domain. This
layer will be made of an ”absorbing material” whose behavior remains described
with the help of partial differential equations and inside which the waves are
damped (hopefully exponentially fast) during their propagation. In such a case,
the boundary condition that has to be prescribed at the external boundary of the
absorbing layer has no particular importance as soon as it leads to a well posed
problem...

The idea, physically rather natural, of absorbing layers has ﬁrst been introduced by
engineers at the beginning of the 70’s. The idea was to join the physical non absorbing
domain to an absorbing medium of physical nature (typically, in electromagnetism one
will use a conductive material, in mechanics a visco-elastic material, ...). This approach
has been progressively abandoned - during the 80’s - at the beneﬁt of absorbing
boundary conditions for various reasons, in particular because it was not supported
- contrary to ABC’s - by a solid and precise theoretical background but also because
its practical use required what I will cal some ”engineer intuition”. In the mid 90’s, the


--- Page 3 ---
Construction and analysis of Perfectly Matched Layers

7

works of J. P. B´erenger [8], [9], who, for Maxwell’s equations, invented the concept
of Perfectly Matched Layers (PMLs), have revolutionized the domain and replaced the
methods of absorbing layers as a very attractive and powerful alternative to absorbing
boundary conditions. The success of PMLs, whose principle is based on a simple but
very clever idea, can be explained by several good reasons among which

• the fact that PML’s are particularly simple to implement (in particular by

comparison with higher order absorbing boundary conditions),

• the fact that they provide in many applications remarkable performances (even

when the theory does not completely predict it),

• the fact that they can be applied without extreme additional complexity to a great
number of equations (including acoustics, electromagnetism, elastodynamics,...)

However, to temperate any excessive enthusiasm, I will add that

• although substantial progress have been accomplished during the past ten years
(which I will try to show later) the mathematical analysis of these methods is
still not sufﬁciently well understood (at least from my point of view).

• there exist physical models for which they do not work because they lead to

unstable mathematical models.

• the winner of the competition PMLs agains ABCs is not clearly designated yet

and a fair comparison remains to be done.

As many (really many) things have already been written on PML’s, I will choose to
insist in this text on a particular point of view, which I hope to be well adapted to a
reader who is an applied mathematician. More precisely, I will pursue a double goal:

• Give a very introductory exposition of the construction of PML’s, which is
not the one originally the one of B´erenger but better corresponds to my
understanding of the method,

• Give a kind of state of the art in the matter of mathematical results about PML’s,
with a particular emphasis on the works done by my collaborators and myself at
INRIA.

In this spirit, I have chosen to organize the content as follows. Chapter 1 concerns
the 1D case and has essentially a pedagogical motivation. After a brief introduction
on classical absorbing layers, I will present - starting from the classical concept of
impedance adaptation - the construction of PML’s for the 1D wave equation. In this
very simple case, everything becomes quite simple and can be analyzed ”by hand”.
Chapter 2 is devoted to B´erenger’s PML’s for a general hyperbolic system in dimension
2 (once one has understood the two-dimensional case, the extension to higher space
dimensions does not pose any problem). I will show how, from a very mathematical
and formal idea - the use of a ”complex” (in the sense of imaginary numbers) change
of variable - one can derive PML’s that generalize the ones proposed by B´erenger for
Maxwell’s equations. In a second step, I will restrict myself to the 2D acoustic wave

equation on which I will explain in detail the absorption mechanism for plane waves,
the treatment of corners, the interest of a variable (in space) absorption coefﬁcient,...
The chapter 3, which concerns the mathematical analysis of PML models, will report
more of some of my recent research. After having recalled the concepts of well-
posedness and stability, I will present some results from the literature. These results are
incomplete. Some of them enlighten some instability for certain classes of equations
which are however of real interest for applications. Finally, some open problems will

    10	
    11	\begin{abstract}
    12	This note is a self-contained source problem for an Iteris run.  The system to be analyzed is the two-dimensional TM Maxwell--PML model with polarization \(P\), PML auxiliary variables \(P_{z,1},P_{z,2},Q_x,Q_y\), and perfectly conducting boundary condition.  The first target is to find a genuinely monotone decreasing energy functional in two space dimensions.  If such a monotone energy cannot be found, the fallback target is to find a positive energy functional that proves boundedness/no abnormal long-time growth, in the same spirit as the long-time-stability role of MPML.  The non-fractional case should be understood as the special case \(\alpha=1\) of the displayed polarization law.
    13	\end{abstract}
    14	
    15	\section{Primary Goal}
    16	
    17	Let \(\Om\subset\R^2\) be a rectangular computational domain containing a physical region and a PML layer.  The absorption parameters are
    18	\[
    19	  \sx=\sx(x)\ge0,\qquad \sy=\sy(y)\ge0,
    20	\]
    21	or, in a harder variant,
    22	\[
    23	  \sx=\sx(x,y)\ge0,\qquad \sy=\sy(x,y)\ge0.
    24	\]
    25	The main goal is to analyze the two-dimensional system in Section~\ref{sec:model} and construct an energy functional \(\Ecal(t)\).
    26	
    27	\begin{enumerate}
    28	\item \textbf{Strong target: monotone decreasing energy.}
    29	Find a positive energy functional such that
    30	\[
    31	  \frac{\dd}{\dd t}\Ecal(t)=-\Dcal(t)\le0.
    32	\]
    33	This is the preferred outcome.
    34	\item \textbf{Fallback target: bounded/non-growing energy.}
    35	If no monotone energy can be found, find a positive energy functional that rules out abnormal growth from the PML layer, for example
    36	\[
    37	  \Ecal(t)\le C\,\Ecal(0)
    38	\]
    39	with \(C\) independent of long time if possible.  If only a Gronwall estimate
    40	\[
    41	  \frac{\dd}{\dd t}\Ecal(t)\le C_\sigma\Ecal(t)
    42	\]
    43	is available, identify the precise terms responsible for the possible growth and whether they are coefficient-gradient terms, corner-PML terms, or algebraic sign-indefinite terms.
    44	\item \textbf{Useful obstruction.}
    45	If the strong target fails for natural quadratic energies, prove or at least sharply identify the obstruction.  An obstruction result is valuable if it explains which part of the PML coupling prevents monotonicity.
    46	\end{enumerate}
    47	
    48	The energy may include weighted \(L^2\) norms, cross terms, shifted variables, time-integrated auxiliary variables, polarization energy, fractional-memory energy, and derivative terms if they are mathematically justified.
    49	
    50	\section{Model to Analyze}
    51	\label{sec:model}
    52	
    53	The model is the system shown in the supplied manuscript image.  Write
    54	\[
    55	  E=E_z,\qquad \epsilon_\infty=\epsilon_{r,\infty},\qquad
    56	  \epsilon_s=\epsilon_{r,s},\qquad \mu=\mu_0\mu_r,
    57	\]
    58	and
    59	\[
    60	  \chi=\epsilon_0(\epsilon_s-\epsilon_\infty).
    61	\]
    62	The unknowns are
    63	\[
    64	  E,\quad H_x,\quad H_y,\quad P,\quad P_{z,1},\quad P_{z,2},\quad Q_x,\quad Q_y.
    65	\]
    66	The PML system is
    67	\begin{equation}
    68	\begin{aligned}
    69	\epsilon_0\epsilon_\infty\,\partial_t E
    70	&= \partial_xH_y-\partial_yH_x
    71	   -\epsilon_\infty(\sx+\sy)E
    72	   -\partial_tP-\frac{\sx+\sy}{\epsilon_0}P
    73	   +P_{z,1}+P_{z,2},\\
    74	\mu\,\partial_tH_x
    75	&= -\partial_yE-\mu\frac{\sy-\sx}{\epsilon_0}H_x+Q_x,\\
    76	\mu\,\partial_tH_y
    77	&= \partial_xE-\mu\frac{\sx-\sy}{\epsilon_0}H_y+Q_y,\\
    78	P+\tau^\alpha\partial_t^\alpha P
    79	&=\chi E,\\
    80	\partial_tP_{z,1}
    81	&=-\frac{\epsilon_\infty}{\epsilon_0}\sx\sy E,\\
    82	\partial_tP_{z,2}
    83	&=-\frac{\sx\sy}{\epsilon_0^2}P,\\
    84	\partial_tQ_x
    85	&=-\frac{\sx}{\epsilon_0}Q_x
    86	  +\frac{\mu\sx(\sy-\sx)}{\epsilon_0^2}H_x,\\
    87	\partial_tQ_y
    88	&=-\frac{\sy}{\epsilon_0}Q_y
    89	  +\frac{\mu\sy(\sx-\sy)}{\epsilon_0^2}H_y.
    90	\end{aligned}
    91	\label{eq:main-model}
    92	\end{equation}
    93	Here \(\partial_t^\alpha\) should be interpreted as a Caputo-type fractional derivative when \(0<\alpha<1\).  The non-fractional case requested by the user is the case
    94	\[
    95	  \alpha=1,\qquad
    96	  P+\tau\partial_tP=\chi E.
    97	\]
    98	Thus the first stage of the analysis should use \(\alpha=1\), not a model with \(P\) removed.
    99	
   100	The boundary condition is the perfectly conducting boundary condition
   101	\[
   102	  \widehat n\times E=0\qquad\text{on }\partial\Om.
   103	\]
   104	For the two-dimensional TM model this should be interpreted as
   105	\[
   106	  E=E_z=0\qquad\text{on }\partial\Om,
   107	\]
   108	so that the Maxwell principal part has no positive boundary contribution.  If a proof uses a different boundary condition, it must state that choice explicitly.
   109	
   110	\begin{remark}
   111	The parameters \(\epsilon_0,\epsilon_\infty,\epsilon_s,\mu,\tau\) are positive, and \(\chi>0\) when \(\epsilon_s>\epsilon_\infty\).  The absorption parameters are time-independent and nonnegative.  The first serious cases to analyze are constant \(\sx,\sy\), then separated variable coefficients \(\sx(x),\sy(y)\), and only then general \(\sx(x,y),\sy(x,y)\).
   112	\end{remark}
   113	
   114	\section{First Energy Balance to Verify}
   115	
   116	Start with the electromagnetic part
   117	\[
   118	  \Ecal_{\rm em}(t)=\frac12\int_\Om
   119	  \left(\epsilon_0\epsilon_\infty E^2+\mu H_x^2+\mu H_y^2\right)\dd x\dd y.
   120	\]
   121	
   122	\begin{task}[Check the electromagnetic energy derivative]
   123	Using \eqref{eq:main-model} and the PEC boundary condition, verify that the Maxwell principal part cancels by integration by parts, and that
   124	\[
   125	\begin{aligned}
   126	\frac{\dd}{\dd t}\Ecal_{\rm em}
   127	=\int_\Om\Big[
   128	&-\epsilon_\infty(\sx+\sy)E^2
   129	-E\partial_tP
   130	-\frac{\sx+\sy}{\epsilon_0}EP
   131	+E(P_{z,1}+P_{z,2})\\
   132	&-\frac{\mu}{\epsilon_0}(\sy-\sx)H_x^2
   133	-\frac{\mu}{\epsilon_0}(\sx-\sy)H_y^2
   134	+H_xQ_x+H_yQ_y
   135	\Big]\dd x\dd y .
   136	\end{aligned}
   137	\label{eq:em-balance}
   138	\]
   139	The terms involving \(H_x,H_y\) are sign-indefinite when \(\sx\ne\sy\).  The terms involving \(P,P_{z,1},P_{z,2}\) are the electric/PML auxiliary coupling terms that must be absorbed by a refined energy.
   140	\end{task}
   141	
   142	\section{The \texorpdfstring{\(\alpha=1\)}{alpha=1} Polarization Identity}
   143	
   144	For the non-fractional case \(\alpha=1\),
   145	\[
   146	  P+\tau\partial_tP=\chi E,
   147	\]
   148	so
   149	\[
   150	  E=\frac{P+\tau\partial_tP}{\chi}.
   151	\]
   152	This gives the useful identity
   153	\begin{equation}
   154	  E\,\partial_tP
   155	  =\frac{1}{2\chi}\frac{\dd}{\dd t}\|P\|_{L^2(\Om)}^2
   156	   +\frac{\tau}{\chi}\|\partial_tP\|_{L^2(\Om)}^2.
   157	\label{eq:alpha-one-dissipation}
   158	\end{equation}
   159	
   160	\begin{task}[Use the alpha=1 identity]
   161	Use \eqref{eq:alpha-one-dissipation} to decide whether the energy
   162	\[
   163	  \Ecal_{\rm em+P}
   164	  =\Ecal_{\rm em}+\frac{1}{2\chi}\|P\|_{L^2(\Om)}^2
   165	\]
   166	is the right starting point.  Then identify the remaining troublesome electric auxiliary terms:
   167	\[
   168	  -\frac{\sx+\sy}{\epsilon_0}EP,\qquad
   169	  E P_{z,1},\qquad
   170	  E P_{z,2},\qquad
   171	  \partial_tP_{z,1},\qquad
   172	  \partial_tP_{z,2}.
   173	\]
   174	Try to absorb them using cross terms, shifted variables, or time-integrated variables.
   175	\end{task}
